content_html:
Run 100 Claude Code or Codex sessions like 5.
The hub keeps them in order, hands the work out and brings you only the decisions, in your browser or in Telegram.

Quick start · Why · Features · How it works · FAQ · Security · Changelog

Experimental, and honest about it. The hub drives Claude Code or Codex sessions (it brings its own copy of the program; you sign in to your Claude account, or to Codex) with no prompt per action, so treat it like a shell on your machine. It runs on your computer or your own server, and nothing is sent anywhere you did not turn on. Not affiliated with Anthropic. Read SECURITY.md before you run it anywhere that matters.

Quick start

The usual way is one line in a terminal:

curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash     # macOS 13.5+, Linux (glibc 2.28+)
irm https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows 10/11, in PowerShell

A team's own build has its own line, with the team's build key in it: take that whole line from your team's chat.

Nothing has to be installed first and no administrator rights are needed, except on Linux without git: there the line installs it through the system's package manager with sudo, so use an account that has sudo or install git first. The line puts the hub's own environment (Python, Node, gh, ffmpeg; git too on macOS and Windows), the hub's code, its service and the hub command into your user folder, then opens the page. The hub installs Claude Code and a browser for agents itself; what is left for you is "Sign in to Claude" on the band above the page. To work on Codex instead, choose "Sign in to Codex" there: the hub restarts on Codex and installs its CLI by itself (Codex). See One path for updates and your own edits.

Or ask your agent to do it. Open Claude Code or Codex in any folder and paste:

Install Hub for me with its one-line installer. On macOS or Linux run:
curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash. On Windows, in PowerShell, run:
irm https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.ps1 | iex. Do not clone the repository and do not run it as root.
If the command times out, run it again: it continues. When it finishes, open http://127.0.0.1:8787/ and
check that the page answers.

Then open the page and write the hub a task in plain words. Telegram, voice and phone access turn on when you need them.

On a cloud server

To try the hub away from your own computer, give it a virtual machine: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, or Debian 12 or 13, x86_64 (Ubuntu on arm64 works too, without Chrome for the agents), 8 GB of memory (3.5 GB at least), 20 GB of disk, your SSH key. When you create it, paste this into its "user data" field:

#!/bin/bash
curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash -s -- --server --yes
Cloud Where the field is Tested
Hetzner Cloud Create server → Cloud config Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Debian 12 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64
DigitalOcean Create Droplet → Advanced options → Add initialization scripts Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13, x86_64
AWS EC2 Launch instance → Advanced details → User data Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64, Debian 12 x86_64
AWS Lightsail Create instance → Add launch script not yet
Azure Create a virtual machine → Advanced → Custom data not yet
Google Cloud Create instance → Advanced → Metadata, key user-data (not startup-script, which runs at every boot) not yet

"Tested" means the line ran from that field on a new machine, the page answered through the SSH tunnel, and it answered again after a reboot with nobody signed in.

A machine that is already running takes the same line by SSH, as root or as a user with sudo without a password (curl -fsSL … | bash -s -- --server); a team's own build — its own line with -s -- --server added. The line makes a user hub without a password and without sudo (the hub's sessions run without asking, so they must not get root), installs git, Google Chrome for the agents (x86_64) and a swap file on a small machine, lets the hub start with the machine, and installs the hub under that user as above.

Nothing of the hub listens on the server's public address: its page is on 127.0.0.1 (and on its tailnet address, if you connect the server to Tailscale and turn Tailscale access on — see Security). Bring it to your computer with SSH, keep the command running and open http://localhost:8787 there; the command is printed at the end of the install and every time you sign in to the server by SSH:

ssh -N -L 8787:127.0.0.1:8787 -L 8788:127.0.0.1:8788 hub@<server address>

On the page, "Sign in to Claude" (or "Sign in to Codex") gives a link and a field for the code. From a phone, use the hub's Telegram bot (sudo -iu hub hub-telegram token on the server), or your own domain in Cloudflare (hub remote cloudflare setup).

The cloud can read the machine's disk and its snapshots, the Claude sign-in included: before you delete the machine, run sudo -iu hub claude auth logout. Deleting the machine removes everything; to keep the machine and remove the hub, run the line again with --server --remove (it takes off only what --server put on: the user hub with its home folder, the swap file, the login message; the packages stay).

One path

Every hub is installed by the one line and updated by its packages; a git clone of the core is only for the people who write the core. The full Hub Developer, the session that changes the hub's code for you and sends fixes, works the same on a hub from the line.

  • Updates come in the background, on one channel: every 6 hours the hub looks for a new version, downloads it, checks its sum and its file list and puts it next to the running one, then asks you to restart ("Restart" on the page and in Telegram; not pressed — it starts at the next restart). If the hub does not come up on it within 3 minutes, the watchdog of the previous version puts that one back. A team's build also reports the failed update to its developers: "About the hub" (Settings → About) says what goes and has the switch (update.report: false).
  • Your settings, plugins and own modules survive every update with no work.
  • The core's code: the Hub Developer edits it in a working copy in the state folder, ~/.hub-core/own/core (hub app src) — a git clone of your release's commit when the machine has access to the repository (with the tests), else the release's own files without tests. Your edits are commits of its branch local; hub app apply builds the hub's code of them with the release's own factory and asks you to restart. A build that does not come up goes back to the clean release by itself; "Return the released" in "About the hub" takes the edits off.
  • An update installs the clean release: your edits stay in the working copy and are not carried over by themselves. Need them still — ask the Hub Developer to put them back or to make a pull request of them (with access to the repository; without it, it files an issue).
  • A hub from git keeps working as it did. The line run on its machine asks whether to move it (sessions, journal, settings, plugins and own modules stay); hub app undo puts it back on its clone within 14 days. With no terminal to ask in, the line changes nothing there and exits with code 3, naming --move and --stay (curl … | bash -s -- --move).

Why a hub

One Claude Code or Codex session is a chat. Ten of them are a mess: which one is stuck, which one waits for you, who told whom what. The hub is the dispatcher. It keeps sessions alive, delivers messages to them, brings you their questions and results, and remembers tasks.

What it is not:

  • Not a sandbox. Sessions run with the tools you give them. The hub adds order, not walls (SECURITY.md).
  • Not a replacement for Claude Code or Codex. Every session is a real Claude Code (or Codex) process that you could open yourself.
  • Not a cloud service. The hub runs on your computer or on your own server, and your code and credentials stay there. The one shared piece is the optional relay that lets hubs talk to each other: it passes their messages without seeing the text, and you can run your own.

What you get

A team, not a chat. You talk to one coordinator session in plain words. It decides who does what, starts the right session and brings the result back. Permanent agents have their own area, tools and notes; short-lived executors work on one task in their own git worktree, report, and go to sleep with their conversation intact.

One feed, with what needs you on top. Every session in one list; the Now tab shows only what waits for you, what is new, what is working. A question from a session arrives as a card with buttons, on the page and in Telegram.

Your phone is a full client. Telegram brings results and questions to your chat; a reply goes to the session that asked. Questions come with buttons, /status shows who works on what. The page itself works on a phone, and reaches it through your Tailscale network without opening any port.

Messages arrive, in order. A message to a busy session waits for the end of its turn and is not lost; an urgent one ("stop, don't touch production") gets through in the middle of a turn. You see whether it was delivered.

It watches itself. An event journal is the single source of truth and the state is a pure function of it. A watchdog notices loops, silent sessions and sessions that repeat the same error. A restart waits until everyone is free, and a session that fell is started again with its conversation.

Extend it without touching the code. Skill sets, MCP servers, your own processes, tabs on the page and themes live in your own folder and do not conflict with updates (EXTENDING.md).

Secrets agents use without seeing them. Settings → Secrets keeps passwords and API keys sealed (AES-256-GCM, the key outside the hub's folder: Keychain, DPAPI, or a file in the settings folder on Linux). An agent puts one into a login field or a command with hub secret fill / hub secret exec and never sees the value; every use is a line in the feed. On for every hub (secrets.enabled: false turns it off); it guards against leaks by accident, not against a session set on getting a value.

One hub or several. Settings → General → Hubs on this computer adds another hub beside this one, with its own folders, service and page (hub instance new <name>), and each hub can have its own password and its own engine, Claude Code or Codex (below). Hubs of different people can be linked by an invitation (Settings → External hubs) so their agents write to each other, encrypted; it is off until you make or accept one. A hub installed by the line above links through the public relay its install names, with nothing to set: the relay sees which hub writes to which and when, never the text. A hub from git pastes that relay's line from v1/relay.json into "Accept an invitation". Your own relay instead: one command on your server (relay/README.md), its line pasted there before the first link.

More: files of your projects in the browser, a scheduler for recurring jobs, voice input, a separate browser per session, an "I am away" mode with a summary when you are back, a catalog of tools with a risk label on each, a "Usage" page in the ☰ menu (Claude limits with a forecast, what the sessions spent), and Settings → Look for the page's theme and text size.

Codex

Codex is the hub's second engine, on a par with Claude Code. The engine is a setting of the whole hub: every session of a hub, the coordinator and the executors included, runs on one of them. Choose it:

  • on the band above the page of a new hub: "Sign in to Codex" instead of "Sign in to Claude" (the hub restarts on Codex and installs the Codex CLI from OpenAI's releases when the computer has none; hub setup codex does only that);
  • for a second hub: "Add a hub" → "Engine: Codex" on the page, or hub instance new <name> --engine codex.

The hub keeps Codex in its own folder: its sign-in (a code you enter from any device, hub codex login), settings and conversations are not your personal ~/.codex, and your rules, MCP servers and memory from there do not reach a hub session. Settings → Codex holds that sign-in.

It works the same as on Claude Code: the feed, cards with buttons on the page and in Telegram, delivery with a mid-turn insert, tasks, executors in their own worktrees, the schedule, the watchdog, restarts that bring sessions back with their conversation, MCP servers and their sign-in, skills from the catalog and from the repository, a repository's hooks and bans, the bus liaison between hubs, voice reply, and the "Usage" page with Codex limits and spend in tokens.

What differs, briefly:

  • Models are named codex/<id>, and an effort the model does not have is lowered to the strongest it has; /compact takes no instructions on Codex, and a conversation does not move between the engines.
  • Sessions run in bypassPermissions mode like on Claude Code (Codex: never ask, no sandbox); the other modes map to Codex's approval policy and sandbox. On Windows the modes that need Codex's sandbox set it up by themselves, and a session that cannot get it does not start.
  • Claude-only things are absent on a Codex hub: the Claude sign-in and Claude's model names.
  • The texts of the sessions, and the hub's own short model calls (the watchdog's "does it wait for you", push texts), go to OpenAI.

How it works

flowchart LR
  O([You]) --- P[Web page]
  O --- T[Telegram bot]
  P --- C
  T --- C
  C["Core<br/>journal · state machines · delivery"] --- S1[Claude Code or Codex session]
  C --- S2[Claude Code or Codex session]
  C --- M[Modules and plugins]
Loading
  • The journal. Everything that happens is a line in the event journal. The state is a pure function of it (core/reducer.py), transitions are state machines (core/machines.py).
  • The core (bin/hubd) is the only writer of the journal. The page, the bot, the CLI and the hooks only send facts to its mailbox; the core records them and tells the host what to do.
  • The host (hosts/streamjson.py) starts one claude -p process per session in stream-json mode; on a hub that runs on Codex, hosts/codex.py talks to codex app-server instead, and the core's facts are the same.
  • Modules (modules/) sit on top of the core: the page, Telegram, the scheduler, files, the watchdog, updates and more. The model only reports facts, the hooks only record events, and only the core decides.

Every known failure became a replay test: a recorded sequence of events that no longer breaks. The suite has about twelve thousand tests (tools/test.py); every release is tested on Windows too, and on the Claude Code version it names, which the hub downloads by itself.

Security

Short version; the full text, with what the hub does not protect, is in SECURITY.md.

The page and "Files" have no sign-in unless you set a password. Without one, anyone else who can open 127.0.0.1:8787 on the same machine (another user, a container next to the hub) acts as the operator, and "Files" shows them the whole disk as the hub's user. Install the hub only on a machine where you are the only user, or set a password for every hub of the machine: Settings → General → Hubs on this computer, "Password" (off by default).
What runs Claude Code (or Codex) sessions as your OS user, in bypassPermissions mode (on Codex: never ask, no sandbox): no prompt per action.
What the hub adds Risky tools (money, production, your data, outgoing messages) connect only after your yes; only your words count as the operator's; secrets are masked in the journal; the hub's folders are readable only by you.
Who reaches the page This machine (127.0.0.1). The devices of this machine's Tailscale login only once you turn Tailscale access on (Settings → Modules → Tailscale; "tailnet": {"enabled": false} in hub.json turns it back off). Your Cloudflare Tunnel only when you set it up.
What leaves the machine What Claude Code sends to Anthropic as usual (on a Codex hub: what Codex sends to OpenAI); the update check (a hub from the line: the project's GitHub Pages and release files; from git: git fetch from its source); the plugin catalogs the hub connects by itself, read from GitHub once a day: the project's own catalog, anthropics/claude-plugins-official and openai/plugins; the downloads of Claude Code and the agents' Chrome when the hub installs them, and of the browser's MCP server from npm when it runs through npx; what you turn on yourself (Telegram, the hub bus, Cloudflare remote access, voice). No telemetry unless you switch it on.
What it does not do Isolate sessions from each other or from your files; stop a session that was talked into something by text it read.
Safer setup A virtual machine or container with only the repositories the work needs, a separate OS user, no administrator credentials.

Installation and configuration

macOS, Linux, Windows, and the settings you will want

This is for a hub run from a clone of the core (Working on the core); a hub from the line needs none of it (One path). You need Python 3.12 or newer and git; the clone's origin is also the update source.

  • macOS: deploy/mac/install.sh: a launchd agent, state in ~/.hub-core, settings in ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json. The installer finds a suitable Python or offers to install one with Homebrew, puts hub and hub-telegram in ~/.local/bin and starts the hub through Agents Hub.app, so macOS asks for access to protected folders once, for it. The open release's launcher, Hub by Icons8.app, is signed ad hoc: macOS ties that access to the launcher's build, so after an update that brings a new launcher it asks once more.
  • Linux: sh deploy/install.sh needs no root. It finds Python (or tells you how to install it), offers to download Claude Code into the hub's own folder when the machine has none, writes the settings to ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json, and runs the hub as one systemd user service agents-hub. On a server without a login session run sudo loginctl enable-linger <user> once.
  • Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\install.ps1 needs no administrator rights. Settings go to %APPDATA%\hub-core\hub.json, state to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core, and the hub starts at sign-in as the scheduled task "Agents Hub".
  • By hand: bin/hub-up; the page is at http://127.0.0.1:8787/.

Control the service with hub off and hub on, open the page with hub ui, check the setup with hub doctor, restart with hub restart. The coordinator session is enabled by the installers; when you start by hand without them, add it to hub.json and restart:

"hub": {"enabled": true, "name": "hub-core", "cwd": "<state folder>/hub-home"}

Optional features are switched on in settings: Telegram (create a bot with @BotFather; enter its token in a terminal on the machine that runs the hub, not in the chat with the hub: hub-telegram token, paste the token, Enter; then send /start to the bot and run hub-telegram pair <code>; for a team, /start in a group instead: its admins speak for the owner, other members only ask, /here <session> gives a topic to a session), voice (Settings → Modules → Voice: a built-in recognition model chosen for the hub's language, or your own recognition command in voice.cmd), the watchdog (watch.json with a model key). Tailscale access (Settings → Modules → Tailscale, or "tailnet": {"enabled": true}): the page and "Files" also listen on the machine's tailnet address for the devices of its Tailscale login (tailnet.owners names other logins; "tailnet": {"enabled": false} turns it back off). A hub that updates from a release without this switch keeps it on if Tailscale worked there at the update; if Tailscale is installed but not connected then, this is decided when it connects; without Tailscale then, it stays off until you turn it on.

Environment variables from your Claude Code settings do not reach hub sessions, except sign-in and proxy. If your MCP servers need tokens, list their names in hub.json ("user_env": ["SERVICE_TOKEN"]); the values are taken from your Claude Code settings and go to every session of the hub.

To set a variable with its value for hub sessions only, put it in hub.json: "session_env_values": {"CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "sonnet"}. Only CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is accepted (other names are skipped with a line in the log, so secrets do not travel through hub.json); the value wins over the same name brought by user_env, and a core module that sets the variable at session launch (launch.env) may override it. It applies from a session's next start.

Reasoning effort is "effort" in hub.json (low, medium by default, high, xhigh, max); for one session hub session effort <session> high. The model is "model" in hub.json, for one session hub session model <session> opus|sonnet|haiku or a full model id.

On Windows, schedule command jobs (hub schedule add --command) and the pre-checks of session jobs run in cmd.exe. With "schedule": {"shell": "bash"} in hub.json they run in Git Bash (the one CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH names, or bash.exe in the bin folder next to git), with hub in PATH: write them as in Bash, with pipes, $(...) and single quotes. If Git Bash is not found, they stay in cmd.exe with a line in the log. On macOS and Linux the setting changes nothing.

A .deb package with its own environment inside (Python, Node, gh, ffmpeg) is built by tools/package/deb/build.sh; the parts of the app installers for every OS — by tools/package/build.py <platform>.

Uninstall

hub uninstall, run in a terminal (not from a session), takes the hub off the machine the way its installer put it on: it stops the hub (and waits until it has stopped), removes its service — the launchd agent com.hub-core on macOS, the systemd user unit agents-hub on Linux, the scheduled task "Agents Hub" and its folder in your PATH on Windows — and the hub and hub-telegram commands in ~/.local/bin that lead to this hub. It shows the plan and asks before it starts; --dry-run only shows it.

Your data stays: the state folder (~/.hub-core, on Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core: the journal, the conversations of sessions, the schedule) and the settings (~/.config/hub-core, on Windows %APPDATA%\hub-core), so a later install carries on from them. hub uninstall --purge deletes them too, after you type the state folder's name (--yes skips both questions); it refuses a folder that does not look like a hub's.

Never touched: Claude Code and its sign-in, Python, and the clone itself — delete the clone by hand afterwards.

  • macOS: the line the installer may have added to ~/.zshrc (or your bash login file) to put ~/.local/bin in PATH stays; it is marked # hub-core: ~/.local/bin. A second hub installed with HUB_INSTANCE=<name> is removed with its own command, hub-<name> uninstall. The downloaded app goes to the Trash as usual.
  • Linux: if you enabled lingering for the hub, it stays on: sudo loginctl disable-linger <user>.
  • Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\uninstall.ps1 [-Purge] [-Yes] [-DryRun] runs the same hub uninstall and also works in a window where hub is not on PATH yet; use it for -Purge, since the hub command itself lives in the folder that -Purge deletes.

To check a clean install and removal on a throwaway machine: sh deploy/smoke.sh (Linux; a temporary home folder, the machine's own hub is not touched; --here uses the real home and service manager — on macOS only this way) and powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\smoke.ps1 (Windows, only where no hub is installed). Each installs the hub, waits for the page and hub status, uninstalls it with --purge and checks that nothing is left.

Extend

Skill sets (Claude Code marketplaces), MCP servers, hub modules (Module API), page plugins and themes live outside the code of the hub and survive updates. Start with EXTENDING.md. A hub from the line updates by its packages (One path): it does not run the tests on your machine, a release has passed them before it comes out, and update.manual: true makes it install only on "Update". A hub from git updates itself too: it follows main (nightly), everything new at once; the merge and the tests run in a separate copy first (update.enabled: false turns updates off).

FAQ

Do I need a Claude subscription? The hub starts Claude Code with its own copy (the one claude in your terminal is not touched), so you only sign in to your Claude account on the band above the page; on a hub running on Codex, to Codex (with a ChatGPT account, by a code). The hub does not give you access to a model.

Where do my data go? Nowhere except where Claude Code already sends them (Anthropic's API; on a Codex hub — OpenAI) and where you point the hub: a Telegram bot, a git remote, the relay of hubs you linked (it carries their messages sealed, without the text). There is no other hosted part, and no usage reporting unless you switch one on. The one exception is a team's one-line build: an update that fails sends its developers a report, on unless you turn it off — the versions, the step, the error with its paths, the update's logs, the free space, the plugins and modules, the machine's and the user's names and the hub's id; no texts of sessions, no journal, no settings. "About the hub" (Settings → About) lists what goes and has the switch.

Does it run on Windows? Yes, with its own installer and a scheduled task; every release is tested on Windows too.

Can I use it without Telegram? Yes. Telegram is optional; the page is the main way in and works on a phone.

How do I remove it? hub uninstall (with --purge for the data too), then delete the clone; see Uninstall.

Why did a database or server I started from a session stop when the session ended? On macOS and Linux every process a session starts carries the marker HUB_TREE=<session>@<hub>. When the session goes away for good (an executor hands in its work, the session is removed, hub stop), the hub sends SIGTERM to all processes with its marker, then SIGKILL; parking a session and hub restart do not touch them. A daemon that must outlive the session (a container VM such as colima/limactl, a database used by other sessions) should not carry the marker: start it as env -u HUB_TREE <command>, or from the system service manager (launchd, systemd). On Windows the session's processes end with it, and env -u does not exist there.

Is it safe to point at my work repositories? It is as safe as running Claude Code (or Codex) with no approvals there: the hub does not change that. Read SECURITY.md and prefer a disposable machine for anything valuable.

Contributing, community, license

  • Pull requests are not accepted for now, a deliberate decision of a small team; see CONTRIBUTING.md for what helps instead: bug reports, ideas in Discussions, and your own modules and plugins.
  • Found a vulnerability? Report it privately through GitHub, not in a public issue (SECURITY.md).
  • Be kind: Code of Conduct.
  • Licensed under the Apache License 2.0: see LICENSE and NOTICE. Bundled third-party libraries and fonts keep their own licenses: see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.

Working on the core

To run the core from a clone and live on main:

git clone https://github.com/icons8/hub.git agents-hub && cd agents-hub && sh deploy/install.sh

On macOS use deploy/mac/install.sh, on Windows deploy\windows\install.ps1 (details above). Such a hub lives on main (nightly), and you make your edits and pull requests right in the clone. Pull requests from outside the team are not accepted for now (see the first point above).

When it finishes, open http://127.0.0.1:8787/ and check that the page answers. Then open the page and write the hub a task in plain words. Telegram, voice and phone access turn on when you need them. On a cloud server To try the hub away from your own computer, give it a virtual machine: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, or Debian 12 or 13, x86_64 (Ubuntu on arm64 works too, without Chrome for the agents), 8 GB of memory (3.5 GB at least), 20 GB of disk, your SSH key. When you create it, paste this into its "user data" field: #!/bin/bash curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash -s -- --server --yes Cloud Where the field is Tested Hetzner Cloud Create server → Cloud config Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Debian 12 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64 DigitalOcean Create Droplet → Advanced options → Add initialization scripts Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13, x86_64 AWS EC2 Launch instance → Advanced details → User data Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64, Debian 12 x86_64 AWS Lightsail Create instance → Add launch script not yet Azure Create a virtual machine → Advanced → Custom data not yet Google Cloud Create instance → Advanced → Metadata, key user-data (not startup-script, which runs at every boot) not yet "Tested" means the line ran from that field on a new machine, the page answered through the SSH tunnel, and it answered again after a reboot with nobody signed in. A machine that is already running takes the same line by SSH, as root or as a user with sudo without a password (curl -fsSL … | bash -s -- --server); a team's own build — its own line with -s -- --server added. The line makes a user hub without a password and without sudo (the hub's sessions run without asking, so they must not get root), installs git, Google Chrome for the agents (x86_64) and a swap file on a small machine, lets the hub start with the machine, and installs the hub under that user as above. Nothing of the hub listens on the server's public address: its page is on 127.0.0.1 (and on its tailnet address, if you connect the server to Tailscale and turn Tailscale access on — see Security). Bring it to your computer with SSH, keep the command running and open http://localhost:8787 there; the command is printed at the end of the install and every time you sign in to the server by SSH: ssh -N -L 8787:127.0.0.1:8787 -L 8788:127.0.0.1:8788 hub@ On the page, "Sign in to Claude" (or "Sign in to Codex") gives a link and a field for the code. From a phone, use the hub's Telegram bot (sudo -iu hub hub-telegram token on the server), or your own domain in Cloudflare (hub remote cloudflare setup). The cloud can read the machine's disk and its snapshots, the Claude sign-in included: before you delete the machine, run sudo -iu hub claude auth logout. Deleting the machine removes everything; to keep the machine and remove the hub, run the line again with --server --remove (it takes off only what --server put on: the user hub with its home folder, the swap file, the login message; the packages stay). One path Every hub is installed by the one line and updated by its packages; a git clone of the core is only for the people who write the core. The full Hub Developer, the session that changes the hub's code for you and sends fixes, works the same on a hub from the line. Updates come in the background, on one channel: every 6 hours the hub looks for a new version, downloads it, checks its sum and its file list and puts it next to the running one, then asks you to restart ("Restart" on the page and in Telegram; not pressed — it starts at the next restart). If the hub does not come up on it within 3 minutes, the watchdog of the previous version puts that one back. A team's build also reports the failed update to its developers: "About the hub" (Settings → About) says what goes and has the switch (update.report: false). Your settings, plugins and own modules survive every update with no work. The core's code: the Hub Developer edits it in a working copy in the state folder, ~/.hub-core/own/core (hub app src) — a git clone of your release's commit when the machine has access to the repository (with the tests), else the release's own files without tests. Your edits are commits of its branch local; hub app apply builds the hub's code of them with the release's own factory and asks you to restart. A build that does not come up goes back to the clean release by itself; "Return the released" in "About the hub" takes the edits off. An update installs the clean release: your edits stay in the working copy and are not carried over by themselves. Need them still — ask the Hub Developer to put them back or to make a pull request of them (with access to the repository; without it, it files an issue). A hub from git keeps working as it did. The line run on its machine asks whether to move it (sessions, journal, settings, plugins and own modules stay); hub app undo puts it back on its clone within 14 days. With no terminal to ask in, the line changes nothing there and exits with code 3, naming --move and --stay (curl … | bash -s -- --move). Why a hub One Claude Code or Codex session is a chat. Ten of them are a mess: which one is stuck, which one waits for you, who told whom what. The hub is the dispatcher. It keeps sessions alive, delivers messages to them, brings you their questions and results, and remembers tasks. What it is not: Not a sandbox. Sessions run with the tools you give them. The hub adds order, not walls (SECURITY.md). Not a replacement for Claude Code or Codex. Every session is a real Claude Code (or Codex) process that you could open yourself. Not a cloud service. The hub runs on your computer or on your own server, and your code and credentials stay there. The one shared piece is the optional relay that lets hubs talk to each other: it passes their messages without seeing the text, and you can run your own. What you get A team, not a chat. You talk to one coordinator session in plain words. It decides who does what, starts the right session and brings the result back. Permanent agents have their own area, tools and notes; short-lived executors work on one task in their own git worktree, report, and go to sleep with their conversation intact. One feed, with what needs you on top. Every session in one list; the Now tab shows only what waits for you, what is new, what is working. A question from a session arrives as a card with buttons, on the page and in Telegram. Your phone is a full client. Telegram brings results and questions to your chat; a reply goes to the session that asked. Questions come with buttons, /status shows who works on what. The page itself works on a phone, and reaches it through your Tailscale network without opening any port. Messages arrive, in order. A message to a busy session waits for the end of its turn and is not lost; an urgent one ("stop, don't touch production") gets through in the middle of a turn. You see whether it was delivered. It watches itself. An event journal is the single source of truth and the state is a pure function of it. A watchdog notices loops, silent sessions and sessions that repeat the same error. A restart waits until everyone is free, and a session that fell is started again with its conversation. Extend it without touching the code. Skill sets, MCP servers, your own processes, tabs on the page and themes live in your own folder and do not conflict with updates (EXTENDING.md). Secrets agents use without seeing them. Settings → Secrets keeps passwords and API keys sealed (AES-256-GCM, the key outside the hub's folder: Keychain, DPAPI, or a file in the settings folder on Linux). An agent puts one into a login field or a command with hub secret fill / hub secret exec and never sees the value; every use is a line in the feed. On for every hub (secrets.enabled: false turns it off); it guards against leaks by accident, not against a session set on getting a value. One hub or several. Settings → General → Hubs on this computer adds another hub beside this one, with its own folders, service and page (hub instance new ), and each hub can have its own password and its own engine, Claude Code or Codex (below). Hubs of different people can be linked by an invitation (Settings → External hubs) so their agents write to each other, encrypted; it is off until you make or accept one. A hub installed by the line above links through the public relay its install names, with nothing to set: the relay sees which hub writes to which and when, never the text. A hub from git pastes that relay's line from v1/relay.json into "Accept an invitation". Your own relay instead: one command on your server (relay/README.md), its line pasted there before the first link. More: files of your projects in the browser, a scheduler for recurring jobs, voice input, a separate browser per session, an "I am away" mode with a summary when you are back, a catalog of tools with a risk label on each, a "Usage" page in the ☰ menu (Claude limits with a forecast, what the sessions spent), and Settings → Look for the page's theme and text size. Codex Codex is the hub's second engine, on a par with Claude Code. The engine is a setting of the whole hub: every session of a hub, the coordinator and the executors included, runs on one of them. Choose it: on the band above the page of a new hub: "Sign in to Codex" instead of "Sign in to Claude" (the hub restarts on Codex and installs the Codex CLI from OpenAI's releases when the computer has none; hub setup codex does only that); for a second hub: "Add a hub" → "Engine: Codex" on the page, or hub instance new --engine codex. The hub keeps Codex in its own folder: its sign-in (a code you enter from any device, hub codex login), settings and conversations are not your personal ~/.codex, and your rules, MCP servers and memory from there do not reach a hub session. Settings → Codex holds that sign-in. It works the same as on Claude Code: the feed, cards with buttons on the page and in Telegram, delivery with a mid-turn insert, tasks, executors in their own worktrees, the schedule, the watchdog, restarts that bring sessions back with their conversation, MCP servers and their sign-in, skills from the catalog and from the repository, a repository's hooks and bans, the bus liaison between hubs, voice reply, and the "Usage" page with Codex limits and spend in tokens. What differs, briefly: Models are named codex/, and an effort the model does not have is lowered to the strongest it has; /compact takes no instructions on Codex, and a conversation does not move between the engines. Sessions run in bypassPermissions mode like on Claude Code (Codex: never ask, no sandbox); the other modes map to Codex's approval policy and sandbox. On Windows the modes that need Codex's sandbox set it up by themselves, and a session that cannot get it does not start. Claude-only things are absent on a Codex hub: the Claude sign-in and Claude's model names. The texts of the sessions, and the hub's own short model calls (the watchdog's "does it wait for you", push texts), go to OpenAI. How it works flowchart LR O([You]) --- P[Web page] O --- T[Telegram bot] P --- C T --- C C["Core
journal · state machines · delivery"] --- S1[Claude Code or Codex session] C --- S2[Claude Code or Codex session] C --- M[Modules and plugins] Loading The journal. Everything that happens is a line in the event journal. The state is a pure function of it (core/reducer.py), transitions are state machines (core/machines.py). The core (bin/hubd) is the only writer of the journal. The page, the bot, the CLI and the hooks only send facts to its mailbox; the core records them and tells the host what to do. The host (hosts/streamjson.py) starts one claude -p process per session in stream-json mode; on a hub that runs on Codex, hosts/codex.py talks to codex app-server instead, and the core's facts are the same. Modules (modules/) sit on top of the core: the page, Telegram, the scheduler, files, the watchdog, updates and more. The model only reports facts, the hooks only record events, and only the core decides. Every known failure became a replay test: a recorded sequence of events that no longer breaks. The suite has about twelve thousand tests (tools/test.py); every release is tested on Windows too, and on the Claude Code version it names, which the hub downloads by itself. Security Short version; the full text, with what the hub does not protect, is in SECURITY.md. The page and "Files" have no sign-in unless you set a password. Without one, anyone else who can open 127.0.0.1:8787 on the same machine (another user, a container next to the hub) acts as the operator, and "Files" shows them the whole disk as the hub's user. Install the hub only on a machine where you are the only user, or set a password for every hub of the machine: Settings → General → Hubs on this computer, "Password" (off by default). What runs Claude Code (or Codex) sessions as your OS user, in bypassPermissions mode (on Codex: never ask, no sandbox): no prompt per action. What the hub adds Risky tools (money, production, your data, outgoing messages) connect only after your yes; only your words count as the operator's; secrets are masked in the journal; the hub's folders are readable only by you. Who reaches the page This machine (127.0.0.1). The devices of this machine's Tailscale login only once you turn Tailscale access on (Settings → Modules → Tailscale; "tailnet": {"enabled": false} in hub.json turns it back off). Your Cloudflare Tunnel only when you set it up. What leaves the machine What Claude Code sends to Anthropic as usual (on a Codex hub: what Codex sends to OpenAI); the update check (a hub from the line: the project's GitHub Pages and release files; from git: git fetch from its source); the plugin catalogs the hub connects by itself, read from GitHub once a day: the project's own catalog, anthropics/claude-plugins-official and openai/plugins; the downloads of Claude Code and the agents' Chrome when the hub installs them, and of the browser's MCP server from npm when it runs through npx; what you turn on yourself (Telegram, the hub bus, Cloudflare remote access, voice). No telemetry unless you switch it on. What it does not do Isolate sessions from each other or from your files; stop a session that was talked into something by text it read. Safer setup A virtual machine or container with only the repositories the work needs, a separate OS user, no administrator credentials. Installation and configuration macOS, Linux, Windows, and the settings you will want This is for a hub run from a clone of the core (Working on the core); a hub from the line needs none of it (One path). You need Python 3.12 or newer and git; the clone's origin is also the update source. macOS: deploy/mac/install.sh: a launchd agent, state in ~/.hub-core, settings in ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json. The installer finds a suitable Python or offers to install one with Homebrew, puts hub and hub-telegram in ~/.local/bin and starts the hub through Agents Hub.app, so macOS asks for access to protected folders once, for it. The open release's launcher, Hub by Icons8.app, is signed ad hoc: macOS ties that access to the launcher's build, so after an update that brings a new launcher it asks once more. Linux: sh deploy/install.sh needs no root. It finds Python (or tells you how to install it), offers to download Claude Code into the hub's own folder when the machine has none, writes the settings to ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json, and runs the hub as one systemd user service agents-hub. On a server without a login session run sudo loginctl enable-linger once. Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\install.ps1 needs no administrator rights. Settings go to %APPDATA%\hub-core\hub.json, state to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core, and the hub starts at sign-in as the scheduled task "Agents Hub". By hand: bin/hub-up; the page is at http://127.0.0.1:8787/. Control the service with hub off and hub on, open the page with hub ui, check the setup with hub doctor, restart with hub restart. The coordinator session is enabled by the installers; when you start by hand without them, add it to hub.json and restart: "hub": {"enabled": true, "name": "hub-core", "cwd": "/hub-home"} Optional features are switched on in settings: Telegram (create a bot with @BotFather; enter its token in a terminal on the machine that runs the hub, not in the chat with the hub: hub-telegram token, paste the token, Enter; then send /start to the bot and run hub-telegram pair ; for a team, /start in a group instead: its admins speak for the owner, other members only ask, /here gives a topic to a session), voice (Settings → Modules → Voice: a built-in recognition model chosen for the hub's language, or your own recognition command in voice.cmd), the watchdog (watch.json with a model key). Tailscale access (Settings → Modules → Tailscale, or "tailnet": {"enabled": true}): the page and "Files" also listen on the machine's tailnet address for the devices of its Tailscale login (tailnet.owners names other logins; "tailnet": {"enabled": false} turns it back off). A hub that updates from a release without this switch keeps it on if Tailscale worked there at the update; if Tailscale is installed but not connected then, this is decided when it connects; without Tailscale then, it stays off until you turn it on. Environment variables from your Claude Code settings do not reach hub sessions, except sign-in and proxy. If your MCP servers need tokens, list their names in hub.json ("user_env": ["SERVICE_TOKEN"]); the values are taken from your Claude Code settings and go to every session of the hub. To set a variable with its value for hub sessions only, put it in hub.json: "session_env_values": {"CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "sonnet"}. Only CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is accepted (other names are skipped with a line in the log, so secrets do not travel through hub.json); the value wins over the same name brought by user_env, and a core module that sets the variable at session launch (launch.env) may override it. It applies from a session's next start. Reasoning effort is "effort" in hub.json (low, medium by default, high, xhigh, max); for one session hub session effort high. The model is "model" in hub.json, for one session hub session model opus|sonnet|haiku or a full model id. On Windows, schedule command jobs (hub schedule add --command) and the pre-checks of session jobs run in cmd.exe. With "schedule": {"shell": "bash"} in hub.json they run in Git Bash (the one CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH names, or bash.exe in the bin folder next to git), with hub in PATH: write them as in Bash, with pipes, $(...) and single quotes. If Git Bash is not found, they stay in cmd.exe with a line in the log. On macOS and Linux the setting changes nothing. A .deb package with its own environment inside (Python, Node, gh, ffmpeg) is built by tools/package/deb/build.sh; the parts of the app installers for every OS — by tools/package/build.py . Uninstall hub uninstall, run in a terminal (not from a session), takes the hub off the machine the way its installer put it on: it stops the hub (and waits until it has stopped), removes its service — the launchd agent com.hub-core on macOS, the systemd user unit agents-hub on Linux, the scheduled task "Agents Hub" and its folder in your PATH on Windows — and the hub and hub-telegram commands in ~/.local/bin that lead to this hub. It shows the plan and asks before it starts; --dry-run only shows it. Your data stays: the state folder (~/.hub-core, on Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core: the journal, the conversations of sessions, the schedule) and the settings (~/.config/hub-core, on Windows %APPDATA%\hub-core), so a later install carries on from them. hub uninstall --purge deletes them too, after you type the state folder's name (--yes skips both questions); it refuses a folder that does not look like a hub's. Never touched: Claude Code and its sign-in, Python, and the clone itself — delete the clone by hand afterwards. macOS: the line the installer may have added to ~/.zshrc (or your bash login file) to put ~/.local/bin in PATH stays; it is marked # hub-core: ~/.local/bin. A second hub installed with HUB_INSTANCE= is removed with its own command, hub- uninstall. The downloaded app goes to the Trash as usual. Linux: if you enabled lingering for the hub, it stays on: sudo loginctl disable-linger . Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\uninstall.ps1 [-Purge] [-Yes] [-DryRun] runs the same hub uninstall and also works in a window where hub is not on PATH yet; use it for -Purge, since the hub command itself lives in the folder that -Purge deletes. To check a clean install and removal on a throwaway machine: sh deploy/smoke.sh (Linux; a temporary home folder, the machine's own hub is not touched; --here uses the real home and service manager — on macOS only this way) and powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\smoke.ps1 (Windows, only where no hub is installed). Each installs the hub, waits for the page and hub status, uninstalls it with --purge and checks that nothing is left. Extend Skill sets (Claude Code marketplaces), MCP servers, hub modules (Module API), page plugins and themes live outside the code of the hub and survive updates. Start with EXTENDING.md. A hub from the line updates by its packages (One path): it does not run the tests on your machine, a release has passed them before it comes out, and update.manual: true makes it install only on "Update". A hub from git updates itself too: it follows main (nightly), everything new at once; the merge and the tests run in a separate copy first (update.enabled: false turns updates off). FAQ Do I need a Claude subscription? The hub starts Claude Code with its own copy (the one claude in your terminal is not touched), so you only sign in to your Claude account on the band above the page; on a hub running on Codex, to Codex (with a ChatGPT account, by a code). The hub does not give you access to a model. Where do my data go? Nowhere except where Claude Code already sends them (Anthropic's API; on a Codex hub — OpenAI) and where you point the hub: a Telegram bot, a git remote, the relay of hubs you linked (it carries their messages sealed, without the text). There is no other hosted part, and no usage reporting unless you switch one on. The one exception is a team's one-line build: an update that fails sends its developers a report, on unless you turn it off — the versions, the step, the error with its paths, the update's logs, the free space, the plugins and modules, the machine's and the user's names and the hub's id; no texts of sessions, no journal, no settings. "About the hub" (Settings → About) lists what goes and has the switch. Does it run on Windows? Yes, with its own installer and a scheduled task; every release is tested on Windows too. Can I use it without Telegram? Yes. Telegram is optional; the page is the main way in and works on a phone. How do I remove it? hub uninstall (with --purge for the data too), then delete the clone; see Uninstall. Why did a database or server I started from a session stop when the session ended? On macOS and Linux every process a session starts carries the marker HUB_TREE=@. When the session goes away for good (an executor hands in its work, the session is removed, hub stop), the hub sends SIGTERM to all processes with its marker, then SIGKILL; parking a session and hub restart do not touch them. A daemon that must outlive the session (a container VM such as colima/limactl, a database used by other sessions) should not carry the marker: start it as env -u HUB_TREE , or from the system service manager (launchd, systemd). On Windows the session's processes end with it, and env -u does not exist there. Is it safe to point at my work repositories? It is as safe as running Claude Code (or Codex) with no approvals there: the hub does not change that. Read SECURITY.md and prefer a disposable machine for anything valuable. Contributing, community, license Pull requests are not accepted for now, a deliberate decision of a small team; see CONTRIBUTING.md for what helps instead: bug reports, ideas in Discussions, and your own modules and plugins. Found a vulnerability? Report it privately through GitHub, not in a public issue (SECURITY.md). Be kind: Code of Conduct. Licensed under the Apache License 2.0: see LICENSE and NOTICE. Bundled third-party libraries and fonts keep their own licenses: see THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md. Working on the core To run the core from a clone and live on main: git clone https://github.com/icons8/hub.git agents-hub && cd agents-hub && sh deploy/install.sh On macOS use deploy/mac/install.sh, on Windows deploy\windows\install.ps1 (details above). Such a hub lives on main (nightly), and you make your edits and pull requests right in the clone. Pull requests from outside the team are not accepted for now (see the first point above). blocks.html_en: Why did a database or server I started from a session stop when the session ended? On macOS and Linux every process a session starts carries the marker HUB_TREE=<session>@<hub>. When the session goes away for good (an executor hands in its work, the session is removed, hub stop), the hub sends SIGTERM to all processes with its marker, then SIGKILL; parking a session and hub restart do not touch them. A daemon that must outlive the session (a container VM such as colima/limactl, a database used by other sessions) should not carry the marker: start it as env -u HUB_TREE <command>, or from the system service manager (launchd, systemd). On Windows the session's processes end with it, and env -u does not exist there.

content_html_zh:
Run 100 Claude Code or Codex sessions like 5. The hub keeps them in order, hands the work out and brings you only the decisions, in your browser or in Telegram.

Quick start · Why · Features · How it works · FAQ · Security · Changelog

Experimental, and honest about it. The hub drives Claude Code or Codex sessions (it brings its own copy of the program; you sign in to your Claude account, or to Codex) with no prompt per action, so treat it like a shell on your machine. It runs on your computer or your own server, and nothing is sent anywhere you did not turn on. 不隶属于人类。 Read SECURITY.md before you run it anywhere that matters.

快速启动

The usual way is one line in a terminal:

curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash     # macOS 13.5+, Linux (glibc 2.28+)
irm https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows 10/11, in PowerShell

A team's own build has its own line, with the team's build key in it: take that whole line from your team's chat.

Nothing has to be installed first and no administrator rights are needed, except on Linux without git: there the line installs it through the system's package manager with sudo, so use an account that has sudo or install git first. The line puts the hub's own environment (Python, Node, gh, ffmpeg; git too on macOS and Windows), the hub's code, its service and the hub command into your user folder, then opens the page. The hub installs Claude Code and a browser for agents itself; what is left for you is "Sign in to Claude" on the band above the page. To work on Codex instead, choose "Sign in to Codex" there: the hub restarts on Codex and installs its CLI by itself (Codex). See One path for updates and your own edits.

Or ask your agent to do it. Open Claude Code or Codex in any folder and paste:

Install Hub for me with its one-line installer. On macOS or Linux run:
curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash. On Windows, in PowerShell, run:
irm https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.ps1 | iex. Do not clone the repository and do not run it as root.
If the command times out, run it again: it continues. When it finishes, open http://127.0.0.1:8787/ and
check that the page answers.

Then open the page and write the hub a task in plain words. Telegram, voice and phone access turn on when you need them.

On a cloud server

To try the hub away from your own computer, give it a virtual machine: Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, or Debian 12 or 13, x86_64 (Ubuntu on arm64 works too, without Chrome for the agents), 8 GB of memory (3.5 GB at least), 20 GB of disk, your SSH key. When you create it, paste this into its "user data" field:

#!/bin/bash
curl -fsSL https://icons8.github.io/hub/install.sh | bash -s -- --server --yes
Cloud Where the field is 已测试
Hetzner Cloud Create server → Cloud config Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Debian 12 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64
数字海洋 Create Droplet → Advanced options → Add initialization scripts Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 13, x86_64
AWS EC2 Launch instance → Advanced details → User data Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, Ubuntu 22.04 arm64, Debian 12 x86_64
AWS Lightsail Create instance → Add launch script not yet
Azure Create a virtual machine → Advanced → Custom data not yet
Google Cloud Create instance → Advanced → Metadata, key user-data (not startup-script, which runs at every boot) not yet

"Tested" means the line ran from that field on a new machine, the page answered through the SSH tunnel, and it answered again after a reboot with nobody signed in.

A machine that is already running takes the same line by SSH, as root or as a user with sudo without a password (curl -fsSL … | bash -s -- --server); a team's own build — its own line with -s -- --server added. The line makes a user hub without a password and without sudo (the hub's sessions run without asking, so they must not get root), installs git, Google Chrome for the agents (x86_64) and a swap file on a small machine, lets the hub start with the machine, and installs the hub under that user as above.

Nothing of the hub listens on the server's public address: its page is on 127.0.0.1 (and on its tailnet address, if you connect the server to Tailscale and turn Tailscale access on — see Security). Bring it to your computer with SSH, keep the command running and open http://localhost:8787 there; the command is printed at the end of the install and every time you sign in to the server by SSH:

ssh -N -L 8787:127.0.0.1:8787 -L 8788:127.0.0.1:8788 hub@<server address>

On the page, "Sign in to Claude" (or "Sign in to Codex") gives a link and a field for the code. From a phone, use the hub's Telegram bot (sudo -iu hub hub-telegram token on the server), or your own domain in Cloudflare (hub remote cloudflare setup).

The cloud can read the machine's disk and its snapshots, the Claude sign-in included: before you delete the machine, run sudo -iu hub claude auth logout. Deleting the machine removes everything; to keep the machine and remove the hub, run the line again with --server --remove (it takes off only what --server put on: the user hub with its home folder, the swap file, the login message; the packages stay).

One path

Every hub is installed by the one line and updated by its packages; a git clone of the core is only for the people who write the core. The full Hub Developer, the session that changes the hub's code for you and sends fixes, works the same on a hub from the line.

  • Updates come in the background, on one channel: every 6 hours the hub looks for a new version, downloads it, checks its sum and its file list and puts it next to the running one, then asks you to restart ("Restart" on the page and in Telegram; not pressed — it starts at the next restart). If the hub does not come up on it within 3 minutes, the watchdog of the previous version puts that one back. A team's build also reports the failed update to its developers: "About the hub" (Settings → About) says what goes and has the switch (update.report: false).
  • Your settings, plugins and own modules survive every update with no work.
  • The core's code: the Hub Developer edits it in a working copy in the state folder, ~/.hub-core/own/core (hub app src) — a git clone of your release's commit when the machine has access to the repository (with the tests), else the release's own files without tests. Your edits are commits of its branch local; hub app apply builds the hub's code of them with the release's own factory and asks you to restart. A build that does not come up goes back to the clean release by itself; "Return the released" in "About the hub" takes the edits off.
  • An update installs the clean release: your edits stay in the working copy and are not carried over by themselves. Need them still — ask the Hub Developer to put them back or to make a pull request of them (with access to the repository; without it, it files an issue).
  • A hub from git keeps working as it did. The line run on its machine asks whether to move it (sessions, journal, settings, plugins and own modules stay); hub app undo puts it back on its clone within 14 days. With no terminal to ask in, the line changes nothing there and exits with code 3, naming --move and --stay (curl … | bash -s -- --move).

Why a hub

One Claude Code or Codex session is a chat. Ten of them are a mess: which one is stuck, which one waits for you, who told whom what. The hub is the dispatcher. It keeps sessions alive, delivers messages to them, brings you their questions and results, and remembers tasks.

What it is not:

  • Not a sandbox. Sessions run with the tools you give them. The hub adds order, not walls (SECURITY.md).
  • Not a replacement for Claude Code or Codex. Every session is a real Claude Code (or Codex) process that you could open yourself.
  • Not a cloud service. The hub runs on your computer or on your own server, and your code and credentials stay there. The one shared piece is the optional relay that lets hubs talk to each other: it passes their messages without seeing the text, and you can run your own.

A team, not a chat. You talk to one coordinator session in plain words. It decides who does what, starts the right session and brings the result back. Permanent agents have their own area, tools and notes; short-lived executors work on one task in their own git worktree, report, and go to sleep with their conversation intact.

One feed, with what needs you on top. Every session in one list; the Now tab shows only what waits for you, what is new, what is working. A question from a session arrives as a card with buttons, on the page and in Telegram.

Your phone is a full client. Telegram brings results and questions to your chat; a reply goes to the session that asked. Questions come with buttons, /status shows who works on what. The page itself works on a phone, and reaches it through your Tailscale network without opening any port.

Messages arrive, in order. A message to a busy session waits for the end of its turn and is not lost; an urgent one ("stop, don't touch production") gets through in the middle of a turn. You see whether it was delivered.

An agent puts one into a login field or a command with hub secret fill / hub secret exec and never sees the value; every use is a line in the feed. On for every hub (secrets.enabled: false turns it off); it guards against leaks by accident, not against a session set on getting a value.

One hub or several. Settings → General → Hubs on this computer adds another hub beside this one, with its own folders, service and page (hub instance new <name>), and each hub can have its own password and its own engine, Claude Code or Codex (below). Hubs of different people can be linked by an invitation (Settings → External hubs) so their agents write to each other, encrypted; it is off until you make or accept one. A hub installed by the line above links through the public relay its install names, with nothing to set: the relay sees which hub writes to which and when, never the text. A hub from git pastes that relay's line from v1/relay.json into "Accept an invitation". More: files of your projects in the browser, a scheduler for recurring jobs, voice input, a separate browser per session, an "I am away" mode with a summary when you are back, a catalog of tools with a risk label on each, a "Usage" page in the ☰ menu (Claude limits with a forecast, what the sessions spent), and Settings → Look for the page's theme and text size.

Codex

Codex is the hub's second engine, on a par with Claude Code. The engine is a setting of the whole hub: every session of a hub, the coordinator and the executors included, runs on one of them. Choose it:

  • on the band above the page of a new hub: "Sign in to Codex" instead of "Sign in to Claude" (the hub restarts on Codex and installs the Codex CLI from OpenAI's releases when the computer has none; hub setup codex does only that);
  • for a second hub: "Add a hub" → "Engine: Codex" on the page, or hub instance new <name> --engine codex.

The hub keeps Codex in its own folder: its sign-in (a code you enter from any device, hub codex login), settings and conversations are not your personal ~/.codex, and your rules, MCP servers and memory from there do not reach a hub session. Settings → Codex holds that sign-in.

It works the same as on Claude Code: the feed, cards with buttons on the page and in Telegram, delivery with a mid-turn insert, tasks, executors in their own worktrees, the schedule, the watchdog, restarts that bring sessions back with their conversation, MCP servers and their sign-in, skills from the catalog and from the repository, a repository's hooks and bans, the bus liaison between hubs, voice reply, and the "Usage" page with Codex limits and spend in tokens.

What differs, briefly:

  • Models are named codex/<id>, and an effort the model does not have is lowered to the strongest it has; /compact takes no instructions on Codex, and a conversation does not move between the engines.
  • Sessions run in bypassPermissions mode like on Claude Code (Codex: never ask, no sandbox); the other modes map to Codex's approval policy and sandbox. On Windows the modes that need Codex's sandbox set it up by themselves, and a session that cannot get it does not start.
  • Claude-only things are absent on a Codex hub: the Claude sign-in and Claude's model names.
  • The texts of the sessions, and the hub's own short model calls (the watchdog's "does it wait for you", push texts), go to OpenAI.

Installation and configuration

macOS, Linux, Windows, and the settings you will want

This is for a hub run from a clone of the core (Working on the core); a hub from the line needs none of it (One path). You need Python 3.12 or newer and git; the clone's origin is also the update source.

  • macOS: deploy/mac/install.sh: a launchd agent, state in ~/.hub-core, settings in ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json. The installer finds a suitable Python or offers to install one with Homebrew, puts hub and hub-telegram in ~/.local/bin and starts the hub through Agents Hub.app, so macOS asks for access to protected folders once, for it. The open release's launcher, Hub by Icons8.app, is signed ad hoc: macOS ties that access to the launcher's build, so after an update that brings a new launcher it asks once more.
  • Linux: sh deploy/install.sh needs no root. It finds Python (or tells you how to install it), offers to download Claude Code into the hub's own folder when the machine has none, writes the settings to ~/.config/hub-core/hub.json, and runs the hub as one systemd user service agents-hub. On a server without a login session run sudo loginctl enable-linger <user> once.
  • Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\install.ps1 needs no administrator rights. Settings go to %APPDATA%\hub-core\hub.json, state to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core, and the hub starts at sign-in as the scheduled task "Agents Hub".
  • By hand: bin/hub-up; the page is at http://127.0.0.1:8787/.

Control the service with hub off and hub on, open the page with hub ui, check the setup with hub doctor, restart with hub restart. The coordinator session is enabled by the installers; when you start by hand without them, add it to hub.json and restart:

"hub": {"enabled": true, "name": "hub-core", "cwd": "<state folder>/hub-home"}

Optional features are switched on in settings: Telegram (create a bot with @BotFather; enter its token in a terminal on the machine that runs the hub, not in the chat with the hub: hub-telegram token, paste the token, Enter; then send /start to the bot and run hub-telegram pair <code>; for a team, /start in a group instead: its admins speak for the owner, other members only ask, /here <session> gives a topic to a session), voice (Settings → Modules → Voice: a built-in recognition model chosen for the hub's language, or your own recognition command in voice.cmd), the watchdog (watch.json with a model key). Tailscale access (Settings → Modules → Tailscale, or "tailnet": {"enabled": true}): the page and "Files" also listen on the machine's tailnet address for the devices of its Tailscale login (tailnet.owners names other logins; "tailnet": {"enabled": false} turns it back off). A hub that updates from a release without this switch keeps it on if Tailscale worked there at the update; if Tailscale is installed but not connected then, this is decided when it connects; without Tailscale then, it stays off until you turn it on.

Environment variables from your Claude Code settings do not reach hub sessions, except sign-in and proxy. If your MCP servers need tokens, list their names in hub.json ("user_env": ["SERVICE_TOKEN"]); the values are taken from your Claude Code settings and go to every session of the hub.

To set a variable with its value for hub sessions only, put it in hub.json: "session_env_values": {"CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "sonnet"}. Only CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is accepted (other names are skipped with a line in the log, so secrets do not travel through hub.json); the value wins over the same name brought by user_env, and a core module that sets the variable at session launch (launch.env) may override it. It applies from a session's next start.

Reasoning effort is "effort" in hub.json (low, medium by default, high, xhigh, max); for one session hub session effort <session> high. The model is "model" in hub.json, for one session hub session model <session> opus|sonnet|haiku or a full model id.

On Windows, schedule command jobs (hub schedule add --command) and the pre-checks of session jobs run in cmd.exe. With "schedule": {"shell": "bash"} in hub.json they run in Git Bash (the one CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH names, or bash.exe in the bin folder next to git), with hub in PATH: write them as in Bash, with pipes, $(...) and single quotes. If Git Bash is not found, they stay in cmd.exe with a line in the log. On macOS and Linux the setting changes nothing.

A .deb package with its own environment inside (Python, Node, gh, ffmpeg) is built by tools/package/deb/build.sh; the parts of the app installers for every OS — by tools/package/build.py <platform>.

卸载

hub uninstall, run in a terminal (not from a session), takes the hub off the machine the way its installer put it on: it stops the hub (and waits until it has stopped), removes its service — the launchd agent com.hub-core on macOS, the systemd user unit agents-hub on Linux, the scheduled task "Agents Hub" and its folder in your PATH on Windows — and the hub and hub-telegram commands in ~/.local/bin that lead to this hub. It shows the plan and asks before it starts; --dry-run only shows it.

Your data stays: the state folder (~/.hub-core, on Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\hub-core: the journal, the conversations of sessions, the schedule) and the settings (~/.config/hub-core, on Windows %APPDATA%\hub-core), so a later install carries on from them. hub uninstall --purge deletes them too, after you type the state folder's name (--yes skips both questions); it refuses a folder that does not look like a hub's.

Never touched: Claude Code and its sign-in, Python, and the clone itself — delete the clone by hand afterwards.

  • macOS: the line the installer may have added to ~/.zshrc (or your bash login file) to put ~/.local/bin in PATH stays; it is marked # hub-core: ~/.local/bin. A second hub installed with HUB_INSTANCE=<name> is removed with its own command, hub-<name> uninstall. The downloaded app goes to the Trash as usual.
  • Linux: if you enabled lingering for the hub, it stays on: sudo loginctl disable-linger <user>.
  • Windows: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\windows\uninstall.ps1 [-Purge] [-Yes] [-DryRun] runs the same hub uninstall and also works in a window where hub is not on PATH yet; use it for -Purge, since the hub command itself lives in the folder that -Purge deletes.

To check a clean install and removal on a throwaway machine: sh deploy/smoke.sh (Linux; a temporary home folder, the machine's own hub is not touched; --here uses the real home and service manager — on macOS only this way) and powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File deploy\smoke.ps1 (Windows, only where no hub is installed). Each installs the hub, waits for the page and hub status, uninstalls it with --purge and checks that nothing is left.

Extend

Skill sets (Claude Code marketplaces), MCP servers, hub modules (Module API), page plugins and themes live outside the code of the hub and survive updates. Start with EXTENDING.md. A hub from the line updates by its packages (One path): it does not run the tests on your machine, a release has passed them before it comes out, and update.manual: true makes it install only on "Update". FAQ

Do I need a Claude subscription? The hub starts Claude Code with its own copy (the one claude in your terminal is not touched), so you only sign in to your Claude account on the band above the page; on a hub running on Codex, to Codex (with a ChatGPT account, by a code). The hub does not give you access to a model.

Where do my data go? Nowhere except where Claude Code already sends them (Anthropic's API; on a Codex hub — OpenAI) and where you point the hub: a Telegram bot, a git remote, the relay of hubs you linked (it carries their messages sealed, without the text). There is no other hosted part, and no usage reporting unless you switch one on. The one exception is a team's one-line build: an update that fails sends its developers a report, on unless you turn it off — the versions, the step, the error with its paths, the update's logs, the free space, the plugins and modules, the machine's and the user's names and the hub's id; no texts of sessions, no journal, no settings. "About the hub" (Settings → About) lists what goes and has the switch.

Does it run on Windows? Yes, with its own installer and a scheduled task; every release is tested on Windows too.

Can I use it without Telegram? 是的。 Telegram is optional; the page is the main way in and works on a phone.

How do I remove it? hub uninstall (with --purge for the data too), then delete the clone; see Uninstall.

Why did a database or server I started from a session stop when the session ended? On macOS and Linux every process a session starts carries the marker HUB_TREE=<session>@<hub>. When the session goes away for good (an executor hands in its work, the session is removed, hub stop), the hub sends SIGTERM to all processes with its marker, then SIGKILL; parking a session and hub restart do not touch them. A daemon that must outlive the session (a container VM such as colima/limactl, a database used by other sessions) should not carry the marker: start it as env -u HUB_TREE <command>, or from the system service manager (launchd, systemd). On Windows the session's processes end with it, and env -u does not exist there.

Is it safe to point at my work repositories? It is as safe as running Claude Code (or Codex) with no approvals there: the hub does not change that. Read SECURITY.md and prefer a disposable machine for anything valuable.
